title: Square Star Pattern
description: Brute force to optimized: per-character printing versus building and reusing a single row, then batching the whole pattern into one output call.

blocks.text: Given a positive integer n, print a solid square made of stars, with exactly n rows and n columns, every position filled with a star character.

blocks.title: Analogy: Tiling a Floor
blocks.text: Picture tiling a perfectly square floor with n rows and n columns of identical star shaped tiles. Every single tile is the same, so once one row of tiles is laid down, the remaining rows are just that same row repeated, no new tile design is needed for the rest of the floor.

blocks.caption: An n by n grid where every single cell is a star

blocks.text: A single row with a single star, the smallest possible square.
No rows and no columns, so nothing is printed at all, an empty pattern.
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about what genuinely varies between different solutions here.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A solid n by n square has n times n characters total, and that total is completely fixed by the shape itself, no algorithm can print fewer characters than that.

Observation 2: What genuinely differs between solutions is not how many characters are produced, but how many separate output operations are used to produce them.

Observation 3: Since every row of a solid square is exactly identical, all stars, there is no reason to rebuild that row's characters one at a time for every single row.

Observation 4: Taking this further, since all n rows are also identical to each other, there is no reason to issue a separate output call per row either, every row can be joined together and printed with one single call for the whole pattern.
That reasoning alone already reframes the entire problem: not "how do I print fewer characters" but "how do I print this fixed number of characters using fewer operations."
The most direct approach uses two nested loops, an outer loop for each row and an inner loop for each column, printing a single star character one at a time.

items: Loop over each of the n rows.
Inside that, loop over each of the n columns.
Print a single star for every column position, one print call per character.
After finishing a row, move to the next line.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: print one star at a time, one call per character

codes.python:
def square_pattern(n):
    for i in range(n):                     # one iteration per row
        for j in range(n):                  # one iteration per column
            print("*", end="")                # print a single star, one call per character
        print()                             # move to the next line after the row


if __name__ == "__main__":
    square_pattern(3)

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Two separate loop variables, one for rows and one for columns, are used specifically because a solid square genuinely has two independent dimensions to walk through, even though both happen to run for exactly n iterations here.

A single star is printed per innermost iteration, deliberately the smallest possible unit of output, so the true cost of one-output-call-per-character is fully visible in this version before anything gets optimized away.
The line break is printed once per row, outside the inner loop, since a row's stars must all appear on the same line before moving to the next one.

blocks.text: This produces the correct n by n square, since every one of the n times n positions is visited and printed.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) individual print calls, one for every character in the output.
Space: O(1) extra space, no string is ever built.

Limitation: issuing one print call per character means n squared separate output operations, and every one of those calls carries its own overhead. Since every row of this particular pattern looks exactly the same, that row can be built once and reused, instead of being reconstructed character by character on every single row.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why printing one star at a time works but is wasteful: it issues n times n separate output calls to produce a shape where every single row looks exactly the same.

What is being rebuilt unnecessarily: the exact same row of n stars, character by character, on every single one of the n rows, when nothing about that row ever changes.

Can the repeated row be built just once: yes, using a direct repeat operation, no character-by-character construction needed at all.

What does reusing it buy: the number of output calls drops from n times n down to just n, one per row, since the same built row string can be printed again and again.

The core idea: build the row of stars once, then print that same string n times.

Build one row of n stars in a single operation, using a direct repeat rather than appending one character at a time. Since every row of a solid square is identical, that one row string can be printed n times, cutting the number of print calls from n squared down to just n, one per row.
Build the row of n stars once, using a direct repeat operation, then print that same row string n times, once per row of the square.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: build the row once, reuse it for every row

blocks.text: This works because every row of a solid n by n square is exactly identical, there is no row-specific information that needs to be recomputed, so building the row string once and printing it n times produces exactly the same visible output as building and printing each row independently, just with far fewer underlying operations. The total number of characters printed is unchanged, still n times n, only the number of separate operations needed to produce them has dropped.

items: The row string is built completely before the printing loop begins, deliberately separating "construct the repeated piece" from "output it repeatedly," so the construction work is never repeated.
A direct repeat operation builds the entire row in one operation, rather than appending one star at a time in a loop.
The printing loop now only ever does one thing, print the same already-built row, once per row of the square, with no per-character work left inside it at all.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) characters are still produced, since that is the size of the output, but only O(n) print calls are made rather than O(n squared).
Space: O(n), for the single row string that gets reused.
10. Further Optimization: A Single Output Call

The row is already being reused n times, so instead of issuing n separate print calls, all n copies of that row can be joined together with newline characters into one complete string, and the entire pattern can be output with a single call.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: join every row into one string and output it in a single call

items: Joining n copies of the row with newline characters between them builds the entire pattern as one single string, before any output call happens at all.
A single output call at the very end is what reduces the operation count from n calls down to exactly 1, regardless of how large n is.

This trades increased memory, the full pattern must be held as one string, for the fewest possible number of output operations, a deliberate space-for-call-count tradeoff, not a reduction in total characters produced.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), the same total characters produced.
Space: O(n squared), to hold the entire joined pattern before the single output call. This trades some memory for the fewest possible number of output calls, exactly one, regardless of how large n is.

blocks.text: Pattern printing problems are rarely about changing how many characters get produced, that total is fixed by the shape itself. The real optimization lever is how the output work is organized: replacing many small per-character operations with fewer, larger ones, first at the row level, then, when possible, across the entire pattern at once.

items: Rebuilding a row from scratch on every iteration even when that row never changes.
Assuming that fewer print calls always means asymptotically less total work, the total characters produced still depend on the shape being printed.
Forgetting the n = 0 edge case, where nothing at all should be printed.

blocks.text: When a pattern has repeated or symmetric rows, pointing out that repetition out loud, and building the repeated piece only once, is a simple detail that shows real attention to how the code actually executes, not just whether it produces the right shape.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you reduce the number of print calls", think: build the repeated row once, then reuse it instead of rebuilding it.
If the interviewer says "can you do this in a single output call", think: join every row together into one string first, then print once.
If the interviewer says "does this change the time complexity", think: no, the total characters printed are always n squared, only the number of output operations changes.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: All three versions produce the same O(n squared) characters, since that is fixed by the shape itself. What changes is the number of output operations: O(n squared) individual calls in the brute force version, O(n) calls in the optimized version, and exactly one call in the further optimized version.

items: Pattern: pattern printing where reducing per-character output calls to per-row, then to a single call for the whole pattern, is the real optimization lever, not the total character count.

Core Idea: every row of a solid square is identical, so building that row once and reusing it n times cuts output calls from n squared to n, and joining all rows into a single string cuts that further down to exactly one call.
Time: O(n squared) output calls for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized version, O(1) for the further optimized version; total characters printed are always n squared.
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(n) for the reused row, O(n squared) to hold the entire joined pattern in the further optimized version.

Most Important Observation: pattern printing problems rarely change how much gets printed, the real skill is recognizing repetition and reducing how many separate operations produce that fixed amount of output.

Interview Difficulty: easy to produce the correct shape; recognizing and eliminating repeated work at the row level, then at the whole-pattern level, is what shows real attention to execution efficiency.
One line memory trick: build the repeated row once, then batch every row into a single output call.
